hess-law-s1.title: Three combustion reactions
hess-law-s1.text: A student wants ΔH° for C(graphite) + 2 H₂(g) → CH₄(g), which cannot be measured directly because carbon and hydrogen do not react cleanly to give only methane. She uses these measured reactions.

hess-law-s2.title: Two routes from N₂ and O₂ to NO₂
hess-law-s2.html:
Two routes connect the same starting substances and the same final substances.

Route A (one step): N₂(g) + 2 O₂(g) → 2 NO₂(g)   ΔH = ?

Route B (two steps):

Step 1: N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 NO(g)   ΔH₁ = +180.6 kJ/mol

Step 2: 2 NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2 NO₂(g)   ΔH₂ = −114.2 kJ/mol

items.q: What must the student do with Reaction 3 to use it toward the target?
options: Reverse it, so CH₄ appears as a product; ΔH becomes +890.3 kJ/mol.
Reverse it, so CH₄ appears as a product; ΔH stays −890.3 kJ/mol.
Keep it exactly as written, since CH₄ already appears in Reaction 3.
Multiply it by 2, since the target has 2 H₂.

why.correct: Match each target substance to the side it is on. CH₄ is a product in the target, so Reaction 3 is reversed: +890.3 kJ/mol.
options: Right: the target has CH₄ on the product side, and reversing flips the sign.
Reversing a reaction always changes the sign of its ΔH; changing the equation but not its ΔH is a common slip.
As written, CH₄ is a reactant; the target makes CH₄.
The target needs 1 mol of CH₄, the same as Reaction 3; it only needs reversing.

items.q: Use Hess's law to calculate ΔH° for C(graphite) + 2 H₂(g) → CH₄(g), in kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Sign: Reaction 3 must be reversed, so its ΔH becomes +890.3 kJ/mol, not −890.3.
Value: Reaction 2 already has 2 H₂, as the target does; use it as written, without halving.
Sign: you reversed the wrong reactions. Keep 1 and 2 as written (C and H₂ are reactants in the target) and reverse 3.

why.correct: Reaction 1 as written (−393.5) + Reaction 2 as written (−571.6) + Reaction 3 reversed (+890.3). The 2 O₂, CO₂ and 2 H₂O cancel. ΔH° = −393.5 − 571.6 + 890.3 = −74.8 kJ/mol.

items.q: Which substances cancel when the three adjusted reactions are added? Select all that apply.
options: O₂(g)
CO₂(g)
H₂O(l)
H₂(g)
CH₄(g)
C(graphite)

why.correct: Everything that is not in the target must cancel: O₂, CO₂ and H₂O. What remains is C + 2 H₂ → CH₄.
options: 1 O₂ + 1 O₂ on the left and 2 O₂ on the right (from reversed 3) cancel.
Made in Reaction 1 and used up in reversed Reaction 3.
2 H₂O made in Reaction 2 and used in reversed Reaction 3.
H₂ stays: it is a reactant in the target.
CH₄ stays: it is the product of the target.
Carbon stays: it is a reactant in the target.

items.q: Why is the answer the same as the standard enthalpy of formation of CH₄(g)?
options: Any answer found with Hess's law is the enthalpy of formation of the last product.
CH₄ is an element, so its ΔH°f is the value of any reaction it is in.
The three measured reactions are each formation reactions.
The target makes 1 mol of CH₄ from its elements in their standard states.

why.correct: C(graphite) + 2 H₂(g) → CH₄(g) is the formation reaction of methane, so its ΔH° is ΔH°f(CH₄) = −74.8 kJ/mol.
options: Hess's law gives ΔH for whatever target you choose.
CH₄ is a compound of carbon and hydrogen.
Reactions 2 and 3 are not: 2 makes 2 mol of water, and 3 starts from a compound.
Right: that is exactly the definition of ΔH°f.

items.q: What is ΔH for Route A, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Sign: ΔH₂ is −114.2 kJ/mol; add it with its sign.
Sign: you reversed the steps. Both are used as written, since they already lead from N₂ + O₂ to NO₂.

why.correct: Steps 1 and 2 add to N₂ + 2 O₂ → 2 NO₂ (the 2 NO cancel). ΔH = +180.6 + (−114.2) = +66.4 kJ/mol.

items.q: Which statement explains why Route A and Route B must have the same overall ΔH?
options: Both routes involve the same number of steps, so they have the same ΔH.
Enthalpy is a state function: its change depends only on the starting and final states.
Energy is created in Step 1 and then destroyed in Step 2, so the two routes balance out.
Both routes happen at the same speed, so they release the same energy.

why.correct: Like the height difference between two places on a map, ΔH depends only on where you start and finish, not on the path.
options: Route A has one step and Route B has two.
Right: both routes start at N₂ + 2 O₂ and end at 2 NO₂, so ΔH is the same.
Energy is never created or destroyed; it is transferred.
Speed is about activation energy, not ΔH.

items.q: What is ΔH for 2 NO₂(g) → N₂(g) + 2 O₂(g)?
options: +66.4 kJ/mol
−33.2 kJ/mol
−66.4 kJ/mol
−180.6 kJ/mol
Reversing the reaction flips the sign of ΔH.
The coefficients are the same as Route A, so the size does not change.
Right: the reverse of Route A, so ΔH changes sign.
That reverses Step 1 alone; Step 2 must be reversed too.

items.q: What is ΔH, in kJ/mol, for NO(g) + ½ O₂(g) → NO₂(g)?

mistakes.why: Value: Step 2 makes 2 mol of NO₂. Halving the equation halves ΔH.
Sign: halving does not change the sign; only reversing does.

why.correct: This is Step 2 multiplied by ½: ΔH = ½ × (−114.2 kJ/mol) = −57.1 kJ/mol.

options: If a reaction is the sum of steps, its ΔH is the sum of the steps' ΔH values.
ΔH of a reaction equals the activation energy of its slowest step.
ΔH of a multistep reaction is the same as the ΔH of its first step alone.
ΔH doubles each time a reaction is split into two separate steps.

why.correct: Hess's law: when equations add to give a target equation, their ΔH values add to give the target's ΔH.
options: Right: because enthalpy is a state function.
Activation energy and ΔH are different quantities.
Each step contributes; the total is their sum.
Splitting a reaction into steps does not change its overall ΔH.

items.q: Given 4 Al(s) + 3 O₂(g) → 2 Al₂O₃(s), ΔH = −3351.4 kJ/mol, what is ΔH for 2 Al(s) + 3/2 O₂(g) → Al₂O₃(s)?

why.correct: Multiply ΔH by the same factor as the equation: ½ × (−3351.4) = −1675.7 kJ/mol.
options: The equation was halved, so ΔH must be halved too.
Right: the target is the given equation × ½, so ΔH × ½.
Halving does not reverse the reaction, so the sign stays negative.
That doubles ΔH; the coefficients were halved.

items.q: Given S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g), ΔH = −296.8 kJ/mol, and S(s) + 3/2 O₂(g) → SO₃(g), ΔH = −395.7 kJ/mol, find ΔH for SO₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → SO₃(g), in kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Sign: SO₂ is a reactant in the target, so reverse the first equation (+296.8 kJ/mol).
Sign: you reversed the wrong equation. SO₃ is a product in the target, so keep the second as written.

why.correct: Reverse the first (+296.8) and keep the second (−395.7). Adding: SO₂ + S + 3/2 O₂ → S + O₂ + SO₃; cancel S and one O₂: SO₂ + ½ O₂ → SO₃. ΔH = +296.8 − 395.7 = −98.9 kJ/mol.

items.q: Use Hess's law to find ΔH for 2 C(graphite) + H₂(g) → C₂H₂(g), given: (1) C₂H₂(g) + 5/2 O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g) + H₂O(l), ΔH = −1300.0 kJ/mol; (2) C(graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ/mol; (3) H₂(g) + ½ O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −285.8 kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Value: the target has 2 C, so multiply equation (2) and its ΔH by 2.
Sign: C₂H₂ is a product in the target, so reverse equation (1): +1300.0 kJ/mol.
Sign: check which equations to reverse. Only (1) is reversed.

why.correct: Reverse (1): +1300.0. Use (2) × 2: −787.0. Use (3) as written: −285.8. Sum = 1300.0 − 787.0 − 285.8 = +227.2 kJ/mol. The 5/2 O₂, 2 CO₂ and H₂O cancel.

items.q: A student reverses an equation for a Hess's law problem and multiplies it by 2, then uses ΔH = −2 × (+150 kJ/mol). What did the student get, and is it right?
options: −300 kJ/mol, which is right: reversing flips the sign and doubling doubles the size.
+300 kJ/mol, which is right: reversing and doubling cancel each other's effect on the sign.
−150 kJ/mol, which is wrong: the reversal alone should change ΔH.
+150 kJ/mol, which is wrong: ΔH stays the same when an equation is rearranged.

why.correct: Apply each change to ΔH: reversing gives −150; doubling gives −300 kJ/mol. A common FRQ slip is adjusting only one of the two.
options: Right: both changes apply to ΔH.
Doubling does not change a sign; only reversing does.
The multiplication by 2 must be applied to ΔH too.
Every change to the equation must be applied to ΔH.

items.q: Which quantity is a state function?
options: The distance a hiker walks to the top of a hill
The enthalpy of a system
The total energy a stove burns while cooking a meal
The number of steps in a reaction mechanism

why.correct: A state function depends only on the state, like the altitude of a place. Enthalpy is one, so ΔH depends only on the start and end states.
options: Distance walked depends on the trail chosen, so it is a path quantity.
Right: H depends only on the current state (substances, amounts, temperature, pressure), not on how the system got there.
That depends on how the meal is cooked, not only on the start and finish.
Different mechanisms can connect the same reactants and products.

items.q: Three methods give ΔH for one reaction: a coffee-cup measurement (−52.0 kJ/mol), Hess's law from tabulated reactions (−56.0 kJ/mol), and bond enthalpies (−61 kJ/mol). Which explanation of the differences is best?
options: Hess's law gives a different ΔH, because routing through other reactions changes the total energy.
The bond-enthalpy value is the most exact, because it counts the actual bonds broken and formed.
Energy lost from the cup makes the measurement low, and average bond enthalpies make that estimate least exact.
The three should agree exactly, so any difference between them means a calculation mistake was made.

why.correct: Calorimetry loses some energy to the room (|ΔH| too small); Hess's law with accurate tabulated data is most reliable; bond enthalpies are average values.
options: Enthalpy is a state function, so the route does not change ΔH.
Bond enthalpies are averages, which makes them the least exact.
Right: each method has its own known limitation.
Real measurements lose energy and bond enthalpies are averages, so small differences are expected.

items.q: Put the steps for solving a Hess's law problem in order.
options: Write the target equation and note the side and amount of each substance.
Reverse or multiply each given equation to match the target, and change its ΔH the same way.
Add the adjusted equations and check that everything not in the target cancels.
Once only the target is left, add the adjusted ΔH values to get its ΔH.

why.correct: Target first; then adjust each given equation (reverse, multiply or both, in either order) with its ΔH; then add the equations and check that only the target is left; then add the ΔH values.
